Large sharks and killer whales prey on them in some marine regions.
Their visible presence can attract wildlife watchers, supporting boat tours and other local tourism businesses.
Researchers use recordings of their underwater sounds to study communication and monitor populations.
A single blowhole on top of the head opens into the respiratory tract and closes underwater.
During rest, one brain hemisphere remains more alert while the other sleeps, allowing periodic surfacing for breaths.
Rows of sharp, conical teeth line both jaws, gripping prey whole rather than chewing it.
Small ear openings lie behind the eyes, with no projecting external ear flaps.
Some individuals wear marine sponges over their snouts while probing the seafloor for food, shielding the skin from abrasion.
Individuals sometimes leap entirely clear of the water, twisting before landing in conspicuous splashes.
In open-ocean settings, some populations travel through deep waters well beyond continental shelves.
In many populations, social groups are fluid, with individuals joining and departing temporary associations.
Blubber beneath the skin stores energy and slows heat loss, helping maintain body warmth in cool water.
Nursing provides calves with energy-rich milk, supporting growth during early life.
